Whopping $1.818 mil transacted price for a Dawson five-room flat — all-time high in Singapore per HDB data
article:
A five-room flat in Queenstown just set a fresh islandwide record for HDB resale prices — by absolute quantum and on a psf basis — when it was resold at $1.818 million ($1,521 psf) on Oct 30, going by HDB’s resale flat database.

Located at Block 96 Dawson Road , part of the SkyParc @ Dawson development, the unit sits on the 40th to 42nd storeys and measures 111 sq m (1,194.8 sq ft). It has a remaining lease of around 94 years.

Ted Wong of ERA Realty Network, who was the appointed agent for the seller, told EdgeProp Singapore that the unit overlooks the expansive greenery of the Dempsey area and saw high demand from prospective buyers.

"More than eight offers were received, with the top three all above $1.8 million," Wong said.

He added that interested parties valued the centrality of the location, abundant amenities nearby, the view of the greenery, and the ample size of the unit.

In Wong’s view, the “relatively low” supply of five-room flats in the estate also contributed to the level of interest and the record-breaking outcome.

The price tag of $1.818 million surpasses the previous HDB resale record of $1.728 million , set in April 2026 when a five-room flat at Block 96A Henderson Road , part of City Vue @ Henderson in Bukit Merah, changed hands. That unit is located on the 46th to 48th floor and spans 113 sq m (1,216 sq ft). Its psf price works out to $1,421.

On a psf basis, the latest SkyParc @ Dawson flat transaction also exceeds the previous islandwide high of $1,502 psf , set in September 2026. That involved a 1,065 sq ft, five-room flat at the neighbouring Block 91 Dawson Road , part of SkyTerrace @ Dawson , which had fetched $1.6 million.

Within Queenstown, the previous record by absolute price was $1.7 million, held by a five-room flat sold in February this year at Block 92 Dawson Road , which is also at SkyTerrace @ Dawson.

At the time, the $1.7 million transaction was the most expensive transacted HDB flat in Singapore.

Source: EdgeProp Buddy , HDB

Completed in 2020, SkyParc @ Dawson serves as a replacement project under the Selective En bloc Redevelopment Scheme (Sers) for residents from Tanglin Halt.

Income-seeking investors often look to Singapore’s largest
real estate
giants for stability and consistent cash flow.
In October 2026, three major CapitaLand-managed trusts –
CapitaLand Ascendas REIT
(SGX: A17U), or CLAR,
CapitaLand Integrated Commercial Trust
(SGX: C38U), or CICT, and
CapitaLand India Trust
(SGX: CY6U), or CLINT – released their third-quarter (3Q2026) business updates.
Since all three trusts report full financial results on a half-yearly basis, these updates did not declare distributions per unit (DPU).
However, they offer a clear window into operational health, portfolio moves, and future growth drivers.
CLAR: Active Capital Recycling and Steady Operational Gains
CLAR holds an impressive portfolio of 236 properties valued at S$20.7 billion as at 30 September 2026.
In its 3Q2026 business update, CLAR did not disclose revenue or net property income (NPI), but operational metrics showed solid improvement.
Portfolio occupancy improved to 90.1%, up from 89.1% in the prior quarter, supported by newly acquired Singapore logistics assets and stronger leasing across its US logistics portfolio.
Rental reversions strengthened to 9.9% for the quarter, with Australia leading at 32.5%, lifting the rental reversions for the first nine months (9M2026) to 9.0%.
Management expects full-year rental reversions to remain in the high single digits.
Portfolio expansion remained active with acquisitions of 5 Tuas Avenue 5 for S$133.9 million and 25 Loyang Crescent for S$504.2 million, at initial yields of 6.6% and 6.9% respectively.
This brought total 9M2026 acquisitions to about S$1.8 billion.
To optimise its balance sheet, CLAR is divesting three Singapore properties for S$281.7 million at a 25% premium to valuation.
If the proceeds are used to repay debt, aggregate leverage would fall from 41.8% to about 41%.
Two redevelopments were newly announced: 29 International Business Park in Singapore (S$264.3 million, expected 1H2030) and Hawleys Lane in the UK (S$76.2 million, expected 2H2028).
These bring CLAR’s ongoing projects – a mix of developments, redevelopments and asset enhancements – to seven, worth S$847.7 million.
Management expects the development and redevelopment projects to deliver stabilised yields on cost of 6% to 8%.
Related articles:
STI Downturn: 3 Temasek-Linked S-REITs to Watch
CICT vs CapitaLand Ascendas REIT: Which CapitaLand Giant Is the Better Buy?
CICT: Major Portfolio Moves Drive Top-Line Growth
CICT is Singapore’s largest REIT, holding a S$28.7 billion portfolio across 25 retail, office, and integrated development properties.
For 3Q2026, gross revenue jumped 15.0% year on year (YoY) to S$464.5 million, while NPI rose 13.8% to S$334.9 million.
For 9M2026, gross revenue and NPI grew 10.0% and 10.4% YoY to S$1.3 billion and S$965.4 million, respectively.
Portfolio committed occupancy improved to 96.1%, accompanied by 9M2026 rental reversions of 4.6% for retail and 7.1% for office.
Top-line expansion was driven by the acquisition of Paragon on 1 July 2026, contribution from the enhanced Gallileo building in Frankfurt, and the step-up acquisition of CapitaSpring.
In 3Q2026, NPI for integrated developments surged 40.8% YoY to S$123.5 million, offsetting an 8.2% decline in retail NPI, which was partly due to the divestment of Bukit Panjang Plaza.
Operations stayed resilient, with 9M2026 shopper traffic up 2.3% and tenant sales per square foot rising 2.1%.
CICT completed the divestment of Asia Square Tower 2 (AST2) on 17 September 2026 for net proceeds of S$2.45 billion at an exit yield of 3.0%.
Asset enhancements remain on track: the S$24 million Tampines Mall upgrade wrapped up in 3Q2026, while a S$160 million enhancement at Plaza Singapura and The Atrium@Orchard targeting 6% to 7% returns has commenced.
Aggregate leverage stood at 39.7%, with the average cost of debt easing to 2.8%.
Related articles:
Keppel DC REIT vs CICT: Which REIT Would I Buy Today?
Unlocking CICT’s Growth Engine: From AEIs to a S$1.1B Hougang Expansion
CLINT: Local Operational Strength Tempered by Currency Headwinds
CLINT is a business trust that owns IT parks, industrial facilities, a logistics park and a data centre across five Indian cities, totalling 22.0 million square feet of completed space.
In Singapore dollar terms, gross revenue for 9M2026 fell 8% YoY to S$206.4 million, while NPI declined 6% to S$161.3 million.
However, these declines were driven by an 11% depreciation of the Indian rupee against the Singapore dollar.
In rupee terms, gross revenue and NPI actually expanded 2% and 4% YoY respectively.
Growth was boosted by higher income from existing properties and contributions from MTB 6 at International Tech Park Bangalore (ITPB), partly offset by lost income from divested assets CyberPearl and CyberVale.
Occupancy held steady at 91%, while trailing 12-month rental reversions reached a robust 23%.
CLINT is positioning itself for substantial multi-year growth, with its development pipeline set to expand total floor area by 46% to 32.2 million square feet by 2030.
Key projects include MTB 7 at ITPB (fully pre-committed to a Fortune 500 firm, completion 3Q2027), CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai (delivering 53 megawatts in 4Q2026), and six forward purchases valued at S$1.0 billion.
Gearing sits at 38.2%, with average debt cost at 5.7%.
Underlying market demand remains strong, as evidenced by record Indian office absorption of 66.4 million square feet in 9M2026.
Related articles:
4 REITs That Could Benefit from Singapore’s S$5B Equity-Market Push
5 Dividend Stocks Set to Shine as Interest Rates Fall
Get Smart: Active Management Keeps the Engine Running
While macroeconomic uncertainties and
interest rat
e fluctuations remain key considerations for real estate investors, these CapitaLand entities continue to show why active management matters.
By selling lower-yielding or mature assets – such as CICT’s AST2 or CLAR’s Singapore properties – and reinvesting into higher-yielding developments and acquisitions, management teams are positioning their portfolios to capture long-term growth while keeping debt levels balanced.
Keep an eye on project completion timelines and

Space Exploration Technologies Corp
. (NASDAQ: SPCX), or SpaceX, has posted its first profitable quarter as a listed company in its third-quarter 2026 (3Q2026) results.
The reason?
A blowout quarter beyond consensus estimates, with
artificial intelligence (AI)
and Starlink doing the heavy lifting.
A Profitable Turn
SpaceX’s 3Q2026 revenue surged 161% year on year (YoY) to US$14.58 billion, while net income flipped from a US$1.05 billion loss to a US$4.40 billion profit, driven by rapid growth in Starlink’s customer base and higher revenue contributions from the Super Intelligence (SI) segment.
The surge in AI rental revenue has won over some analysts, but not all.
Morningstar raised its fair-value estimate for SpaceX but still considers the shares significantly overvalued, trading at roughly twice that estimate.
These improved results are landing SpaceX on growth investors’ watchlists.
Super Intelligence: The New Top-Line Powerhouse
SpaceX’s SI (previously AI) segment delivered a superb 3Q2026 performance, with revenue rising 829.9% YoY to US$7.56 billion, swinging from an operating loss of US$1.72 billion to an operating profit of US$431 million.
Large Grok Enterprise (including Cursor) customer accounts within the SI division – those that already generate over US$1 million in annual run-rate revenue – grew 50% quarter on quarter (QoQ) on a pro forma basis.
Remarkably, the SI segment now generates 51.9% of total net sales, surpassing satellite connectivity as the largest revenue contributor.
Crucially, it’s showing no signs of slowing.
While its active compute capacity reached 1.7 gigawatts (GW) as of 30 September 2026, management targets between 2.5 GW and 3.0 GW by the end of 2026 and around 13 GW by the end of 2027.
To sweeten the deal, management says the newly deployed compute is paying back its cost in less than a year at current rental prices.
That is a sign that, for now, demand is keeping pace with SpaceX’s build-out.
Related articles:
Missed the AI Boom? Here’s How Investors Can Still Benefit from the Next Wave
3 Singapore Stocks Quietly Profiting from the AI Boom
Starlink’s Profitability
While SI dominates the headlines, SpaceX’s Starlink and launch segments provide steady growth and space supremacy, respectively.
Revenue from the Connectivity segment, which houses Starlink, rose 69.5% YoY to US$5.20 billion, supported by an 88.9% jump in consumer subscribers and a US$1.02 billion increase in enterprise and government revenue, led by Starshield (its US government business) and airline installations.
Although average revenue per user (ARPU) for consumers fell 16.9% YoY to US$69 a month, the bigger subscriber base more than made up for it, with consumer revenue up 57%.
Starlink Mobile, its satellite-to-mobile broadband service, performed well, with monthly active users surging 37% QoQ to more than 22 million.
Generating $2.37 billion in operating profit at a 45.1% margin, the Connectivity segment remains SpaceX’s biggest profit engine.
Space Supremacy
SpaceX’s Space Operations 3Q2026 revenue rose 6.1% YoY to US$1.77 billion despite launches falling from 44 to 35, helped by a more favourable mix of customer missions.
That said, the segment slipped to a small operating loss of US$7 million, from a US$259 million profit a year ago, as SpaceX ramped up spending on Starship development.
Notably, SpaceX successfully sent Starship – its towering next-generation rocket – into orbit for the first time on Flight 14 and delivered 26 of its latest Starlink V3 satellites, marking a major milestone.
According to Starlink, a single V3 satellite provides ten and twenty-two times the downlink and uplink capacity, respectively, compared with a V2 satellite, potentially reducing its cost per unit bandwidth, which could in turn drive future margin expansion.
Explosive Guidance vs. Spending Realities
SpaceX reiterated its target of US$100 billion in annualised revenue run rate (ARR) by the end of 2026, while CEO Elon Musk suggested ARR could reach $500 billion to $1 trillion by end-2027, a five- to tenfold increase within a year.
This comes after increased visibility into SpaceX’s compute contract pipeline over the next six months.
Its massive backlog of US$63 billion, of which $42 billion is expected to be recognised within twelve months, also bolstered management’s optimism.
However, behind the rosy guidance lies an immense capital commitment.
Beyond its compute hardware and power build-out, SpaceX is also constructing Starbase, Louisiana.
The new spaceport is designed to handle thousands of Starship flights a year, with its first launch targeted for 2029.
In the first nine months of 2026 (9M2026), its operating cash flow and capital expenditure (capex) stood at US$13.10 billion and US$48.07 billion, respectively, pushing its free cash flow (FCF) into the red.
With its fourth quarter 2026 (4Q2026) capex projected to spike from US$19.59 billion in 3Q2026 to between $35 billion and $40 billion, its negative FCF is expected to worsen.
As of 30 September 2026, SpaceX maintained a decent
balance sheet
, supported by a favourable current ratio of 3.08x and a net cash position of US$51 billion, providing a cushion against its cash burn.

title: Treasuries extend monthly advance as tech giants stumble
article:
(Oct 30): Treasuries gained on Friday, sending yields to their lowest levels in a month, as slumping shares of giant technology companies stoked demand for havens including US government debt.

Treasuries extended an advance that began when Amazon.com Inc and Intel Corp reported quarterly results that disappointed investors minutes after the US stock market closed on Thursday. Most yields were lower by less than a basis point at 10.30am in New York, after having reached the lowest levels in a month during Asia trading hours. The 10-year yield fell as much as five basis points to 4.89%, last seen on Sept 10.

Demand for secure assets also arose from a setback for cryptocurrencies after Binance, the world’s largest crypto exchange, suspended deposits and withdrawals as it investigated a suspected hack. For bond investors, the prospect of tightening financial conditions at least temporarily overwhelmed a jump in oil prices, which has the potential to sustain elevated inflation.

“Bonds are rallying this morning with another safe-haven swoon after the tech results this week,” said Kenneth Crompton, the head of rates strategy at National Australia Bank in Sydney.

Souring sentiment around artificial intelligence (AI)-linked equities has been a primary catalyst for US government bond gains over the past month. The 10-year note’s yield has fallen more than 40 basis points from its Oct 7 multi-year high, and a Bloomberg index tracking Treasury returns has climbed 2% in October, on pace for its biggest monthly advance since February 2025.

See also: US employment cost growth stable, stays below inflation

Short-term Treasuries — which are most sensitive to the outlook for US Federal Reserve interest-rate moves — also drew support from Fed chairman Kevin Warsh’s remarks after the Oct 28 decision to leave rates unchanged. While vowing to bring inflation down to the central bank’s 2% target, Warsh said he was encouraged by progress since its September rate increase.

The Bank of Japan and the Reserve Bank of New Zealand also held off from raising interest rates this week despite elevated energy costs adding to price pressures.

For the Fed’s next decision on Dec 9, traders are pricing in a roughly 80% chance of a quarter-point increase. Before this week’s decision, three hikes by the end of next year were fully priced into swap contracts.

See also: US trade gap jumps to most since March 2025 on capital goods

“Treasuries are willing to remain quite responsive to the vagaries of the sentiment on AI valuations and equity market wobbles,” said Padhraic Garvey at ING Financial Markets.

Several technical factors also are in play for Treasuries in the near term. Because Friday is the last business day of the month, bond indexes are scheduled to be rebalanced, a process by which index-eligible debt sold during the month is added and securities with less than a year to maturity drop out. The rebalancing normally drives a surge in trading as index funds and other passively managed accounts adjust their holdings.

For the Bloomberg Treasury Index, the rebalancing at 4pm New York time is projected to extend its duration by 0.05 year. The impact on the market can be positive or negative depending on how closely index-related buying matches expectations for it.

Also, the Treasury Department’s quarterly announcement of its financing plans on Wednesday will set the stage for any increase in auction sizes, which are viewed as inevitable though the timing is uncertain.

Also looming on the horizon for the bond market are the US midterm elections on Nov 3. Investors are growing skeptical that the potential return of gridlock on Capitol Hill will ease their worries about the US fiscal trajectory the way it has for decades.

But for now, the focus remains squarely on the sell-off in tech stocks as doubts grow about whether heavy AI spending can deliver the profit growth needed to justify current valuations.

The rally is likely to extend as “we did not think that Warsh was especially hawkish in his post meeting press conference, and it seems likely these AI-related concerns will continue”, said Andrew Ticehurst, a senior rates strategist at Nomura Holdings Inc in Sydney.

title: Big Oil scores US$56 bil windfall on war-driven refining spike
article:
(Oct 30): Big Oil reaped more than US$50 billion ($63.9 billion) in windfall profits as conflicts in the Persian Gulf and Russia roiled energy markets and drove refining results to record highs.

ExxonMobil Holdings Corp, Chevron Corp, BP plc, Shell plc and TotalEnergies SE all surpassed third-quarter expectations with combined adjusted net income of US$56.3 billion, driven by an unprecedented fuel-supply crises that drove pump prices to record highs.

Motorists’ pain at the pump is providing outsized profits for oil supermajors while fanning discontent as US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party head into midterm elections that will determine control of Congress. American voters consistently cite the cost of living as a top concern with high fuel prices turning traditional Republican strongholds including Texas, Kansas and Alaska into battleground states.

International oil prices are up almost 60% since the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February, and refining has emerged as an additional choke point in the global energy supply chain. The fighting in the Middle East and Ukrainian strikes in Russia have sidelined about 10% of the world’s fuel-making capacity, handing enormous profits to plants that remain operational.

ExxonMobil’s refining division earned a record US$9.05 billion during the third quarter, almost five times higher than a year earlier, according to a statement on Friday. Meanwhile, Chevron’s refineries raked in US$4.93 billion in profit, the highest on record and four times more than a year ago.

See also: Oil surges on signs US may resume military strikes against Iran

For BP, more than half its US$8.46 billion in adjusted net income came from the unit that includes oil refining and trading. Earlier in the week, Shell and Total also disclosed blockbuster results.

ExxonMobil rose as much as 2.5% in New York while Chevron climbed 2.1%. BP advanced as much as 1.8% in London. Shell and Total also advanced.

Trump has batted away concerns over gasoline and diesel prices, which are higher on average during his second term than under his predecessor Joe Biden, saying they will come down “very soon” at a rally in Texas this week. A few days earlier he praised US oil companies for making “a freaking fortune” for the country, an apparent U-turn after criticising them for “making too much money” this summer.

See also: Bangladesh in talks to buy more American gas, says US ambassador

Yet with the Iran conflict entering its ninth month, the disruptions to global energy markets show little sign of easing despite more ships now passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Until now, markets have leaned heavily on supplies from strategic and commercial stockpiles. But with these buffers running low, price volatility is forecast to escalate.

ExxonMobil, which operates the largest refining system outside China, reported its fourth-highest overall profit in the company’s 156-year history. The company’s adjusted third-quarter earnings of US$4.23 a share were 10 cents higher than the average analyst estimate.

ExxonMobil raised dividends for the 44th consecutive year and pledged to maintain US$20 billion in annual buy-backs.

Chief financial officer Neil Hansen said the profit surge was less a windfall than a reward for ramping up production at a time when it is most needed. ExxonMobil has increased Gulf Coast distillate production 40% since 2019 as a result of heavy investment since 2020, when rivals sold off fuel-making facilities or converted them to biofuel plants.

“The most meaningful response to those higher global commodity prices that we can offer as a company is to pull every lever that’s available to us to increase supply,” Hansen said during an interview. ExxonMobil is “putting more diesel on the market in a very strained environment today”.

Chevron also notched its fourth-highest quarterly profit in company history. Its third-quarter net income of US$5.28 a share was 35 cents higher than the average analyst estimate. The company maintained share buy-backs at US$2.5 billion for the quarter, the low end of its full-year guidance range. For the second consecutive quarter, Chevron executives funnelled windfall profits primarily into debt reduction.

“We don’t react to upside or downside, we don’t move things around,” chief financial officer Eimear Bonner said during an interview. “For now, we are sticking with our longstanding financial priorities and we’re not making any changes.”

The fact that Chevron didn’t bump up its annual share repurchase range “perhaps reflects the optics around bumper buy-backs rather than increasing investment in an energy crisis”, Biraj Borkhataria of RBC Capital Markets said in a note.

Aided by last year’s acquisition of Hess Corp, Chevron increased production year-on-year, allowing it to take advantage of the roughly 34% jump in international crude prices from a year earlier. The Hess deal gave Chevron a 30% stake in Guyana’s prolific Stabroek Block that’s operated by ExxonMobil.

Chevron is on track to produce 300,000 barrels a day from Venezuela by the end of this year, up 20% from a year ago. The company’s costs are less than US$20 a barrel in the country, making it one of the most profitable oil theatres in the world.

Venezuela is “immediately accretive and free cash flow positive”, Bonner said. “We are not concerned with our ability to grow that production.”

title: Binance estimates US$6.3 bil hacked in crypto's biggest heist
article:
(Oct 30): Hackers siphoned off US$6.3 billion ($8.1 billion) from crypto exchange Binance in the biggest heist of the digital-asset industry and the latest in a slew of security incidents afflicting the financial sector.

The world’s largest crypto trading platform suspended withdrawals on Friday and pledged to cover all losses. Binance said in a post on X that about US$3 billion of the assets had been frozen on blockchain networks. In another post, co-founder Yi He said withdrawals were expected to resume by Sunday.

While the full details of the Binance breach have yet to emerge, the incident comes amid growing concern about the risks posed by hackers in the age of artificial intelligence (AI). Other recent cyberattacks have hit prediction market Polymarket, South Korean financial firms Mirae Asset Global Investments Co and Daishin Securities, as well as Japanese currency trading platform GMO Internet Group Inc.

Blockchain intelligence firms TRM Labs, Chainalysis and Elliptic have all pointed to North Korea as behind the Binance heist. TRM called it “the largest crypto theft on record”. The funds drained in the attack were a mix of the largest cryptocurrencies, including bitcoin, ether, and the dollar-backed stablecoins USDT and USDC.

The breach is a setback for an industry that is maturing and seeking to expand into traditional finance. Before now, the biggest publicly known crypto hack occurred at exchange Bybit in February 2025, in which attackers made off with almost US$1.5 billion in tokens.

Notorious previous episodes of theft and fraud among fallen crypto giants such as FTX and Mt Gox set the stage for protracted bear markets, bruises the industry has worked to put behind it in US President Donald Trump’s promised new era of regulatory clarity for cryptocurrencies.

See also: Bitcoin drops below US$77,000 as Binance hack shakes crypto

Largest token bitcoin fell on news of the Binance attack, dropping below US$77,000 for the first time in more than a month. It pared losses later, trading at around US$77,500 at 6am in New York.

For crypto faithful who’d been basking in a two-month-long price rebound, the Binance incident has cast a shadow over the recovery.

“Binance is such a behemoth in crypto that any hit to confidence in them is a hit to confidence in the industry as a whole, especially as people have already been skittish over the increasing cyber capabilities of AI,” said Fredrick Collins, the chief executive officer and a co-founder of crypto data platform Velo Data.

See also: Record Binance hack shows no crypto firm is too big to breach

Binance dwarfs its industry rivals. It holds roughly US$135.2 billion in assets, compared with US$28.6 billion at the second-largest exchange OKX, according to DefiLlama data.

The hackers appear to have exploited how Binance authorises transactions, according to TRM. They seemingly gained access to the exchange’s systems and used internal software to authorise transfers across 10 different blockchains, including bitcoin and ethereum, it said.

“TRM attributes the attack to TraderTraitor, North Korea’s elite hacking unit, based on robust on and off-chain intelligence,” the firm said. “We make this judgement with high confidence.”

Binance said the incident may involve a compromised software engineer’s laptop, among “additional points of breach”. It found no evidence of leaked private keys, it said.

“This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it,” Binance said in a post on X.

An emergency insurance and reserve fund from Binance called the secure asset fund for users (Safu) was established in 2018 to serve as a backstop for customers in “extreme situations”, according to the exchange. Safu is generally maintained at around US$1 billion, but has fluctuated in the past in tandem with market movements, Binance said in 2024.

The two biggest stablecoin issuers said they took steps to freeze affected currency. Paolo Ardoino, the CEO of Tether, said in an X post that it froze more than US$1.5 billion of the stablecoin “related to a potential Binance exchange hack”. Jeremy Allaire, who runs Circle Internet Group Inc, said US$800 million of its coin had been frozen amid “reports of a potential exploit involving Binance”.

To stay ahead of Singapore and the region’s corporate and economic trends, click here for Latest Section

Sentiment was already fragile after a spate of crypto security incidents. In recent months, hundreds of millions of dollars were drained from Bitget, while tampering involving Ledger devices also led to millions of dollars in losses.

“Attackers are operating at unprecedented speed and scale” but “the tools to track and trace operate at that speed too”, said Ari Redbord, the global head of policy at TRM Labs. “Stablecoin issuers freeze within hours. Investigators follow funds across chains in real time.”

Traders had already been bracing for greater volatility in the crypto market this week, with US$11 billion in options set to expire on Friday. This comes days ahead of the US midterm elections taking place next week, when Democrats could potentially retake one or both chambers of Congress and open the door to greater regulatory scrutiny for the industry.

Exchange thefts and malfeasance have been an ever-present backdrop of crypto’s almost two-decade ascent, the most famous of which was the collapse of Sam Bankman-Fried’s FTX in November 2022. In what remains perhaps the most notorious hacking incident, Japan-based bitcoin exchange Mt Gox was struck in 2011. Over time, the hackers made off with tokens worth billions of dollars based on the current market price. Mt Gox eventually went bankrupt.

“It’s a huge damage to crypto because of the consistent successful hacks in the space,” said Tian Zeng, the CEO of crypto hedge fund Third Eye. “The fact that exploits keep happening makes it dangerous in the age of newest AI models being released every two weeks.”

The Binance incident came on the same day event-contract venue Polymarket halted trading on its international exchange for an hour after it said that a third-party software provider was compromised. More than 700 Polymarket users were drained of US$2.7 million in funds, said blockchain analytics platform Bubblemaps, in a post on X. A spokesman declined to comment on the numbers.

South Korea’s second-largest crypto exchange Bithumb was also among the country’s finance firms hit by data breaches this week, with hundreds of customer records affected, Yonhap reported.

title: US employment cost growth stable, stays below inflation
article:
(Oct 30): US labour cost growth held steady in the third quarter, suggesting that the job market is not contributing to broader inflationary pressures.

The employment cost index (ECI), which tracks changes in wages and benefits, increased 3.4% in the 12 months ended in September, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) figures out on Friday. Adjusted for inflation, compensation costs declined 0.4%.

On a quarterly basis, the gauge rose 0.8%.

The labour market has been broadly stable this year, with few layoffs alongside subdued hiring. But many workers have struggled to keep up with rising prices.

“Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little. But inflation remains elevated,” Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh said Wednesday after the central bank decided to keep interest rates unchanged.

Friday’s ECI report showed that growth in wages and salaries for civilian workers edged down to 0.7% in the three months through September, and 3.1% from a year earlier — the lowest since 2021. Adjusted for inflation, wages fell 0.6% in the 12 months through September.

See also: US trade gap jumps to most since March 2025 on capital goods

Private-sector employer costs for health benefits picked up to 6.4% in the year through September, the highest since the end of 2025.

Next week, the BLS will release its October jobs report, offering a fresh look at hiring and wages across the US.

title: Eurozone 3Q growth beats estimates despite slump in France
article:
(Oct 30): The euro-area economy grew at twice the pace analysts predicted, despite an unexpected slump in France and headwinds including elevated inflation and the selloff in bond markets.

Gross domestic product across the 21-member currency bloc rose 0.4% in the third quarter (3Q), Eurostat said on Friday. Performances were mixed among its biggest members as Germany and Spain grew, Italy stagnated and France shrank by 0.1%.

The overall outcome highlights Europe’s broader sturdiness, not just to the Iran war’s inflationary impact but to the heat waves and droughts that marred much of the summer. Still, the European Central Bank (ECB) has flagged downside risks and could yet hike interest rates for a third time in December after standing pat this week.

While inflation hasn’t spread beyond energy yet, officials in Frankfurt are wary. Separate data from Italy and France won’t reassure them, with prices jumping by 5.6% and 3.8% in October, the quickest since 2023 and ahead of expectations.

Inflation in Spain, despite easing a touch as anticipated, remained elevated at 4.9%.

See also: AI darling Taiwan extends economic growth run unseen since 1987

The jump in global bond yields is another drag, with France’s shaky fiscal and political position making it the region’s focal point. Its economy was already the euro area’s major laggard, only narrowly avoiding a recession in the first half amid soft domestic demand, falling investment and as hot weather hurt agriculture.

The outlook is bleak. Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu is in the midst of another parliamentary showdown over austerity, against a backdrop of social and political upheaval before presidential elections in 2027 where the far right leads polls.

“France’s economy is at a standstill due to a unprecedented convergence of external and domestic shocks,” Finance Minister Roland Lescure said on Friday. “It needs to pick up. We need to restore confidence and for that having a budget is essential as that is what will allow us to bring down interest rates.”

See also: Lagarde downplays inflation risk as ECB holds, announces her early exit

German GDP rose 0.2% despite factors including low water levels in the River Rhine. A public-spending spree on infrastructure and defense is generating optimism while carmakers may benefit from a European cap on Chinese hybrid-vehicle imports.

At the same time, Chancellor Friedrich Merz has made fresh efforts to perk up growth through social-welfare reforms and attempts to lure private capital.

“The headline overstates the strength of the economy. National data suggest Ireland accounted for about half of the increase, while the four largest economies grew by just 0.1% on average. With the conflict in Iran unresolved and energy prices still high, we think the bigger drag is yet to come. For now, though, the stronger GDP data reinforce our view that the ECB remains on track for another 25bp rate hike in December,” says Simona Delle Chiaie, chief euro-area economist at Bloomberg Economics.

Italy’s government forecasts GDP will increase 1% in 2026, helping finance some of the tax cuts Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has promised before elections next year.

She’s also asked Brussels for extra leeway of about €28 billion for energy and defense outlays. Any slowdown in growth would complicate other fiscal commitments, including getting the budget deficit below 3% of output.

Spain, whose latest GDP reading was driven by domestic demand and trade, has shown significant resilience, with the central bank listing private consumption, job creation and population growth among drivers.

It sees growth of 2.6% in 2026 and 2.2% in 2027, comfortably above the euro area’s pace. It’s largely shaken off political instability including Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez inability to pass a budget.

title: Bitcoin drops below US$77,000 as Binance hack shakes crypto
article:
(Oct 30): Bitcoin sank below US$77,000 ($98,383) for the first time in more than a month, deepening a sell-off after Binance Holdings revealed a record hack that rattled the crypto industry and renewed questions about the security of customer assets — even at the world’s largest digital-asset exchange.

The original cryptocurrency declined as much as 3.1% on Friday to fall as low as US$76,300. Other tokens, including some that were impacted by the security breach, also fell. Binance’s BNB token has declined about 5% over the past 24 hours to around US$700.

The breach — in which attackers siphoned off over US$6 billion — is the largest crypto theft on record, and delivers another blow to an industry that has spent years trying to shed its reputation for hacks, scams and exchange failures. It’s also putting Binance’s own defences under scrutiny by raising questions about how an exchange of its size — with more than US$135 billion of assets on its platform — could have succumbed to a breach of such magnitude.

Binance on Friday said that it has reserved US$6.34 billion of company funds in the wake of the incident.

“The broader crypto market was already leaning bearish, which is why the sell-off spread so quickly across the board,” said Jeff Ko, the chief analyst at ViaBTC. He added that Binance can absorb the losses.

See also: Record Binance hack shows no crypto firm is too big to breach

Bitcoin and other tokens were already under pressure this week with broader macro forces weighing on the market. Futures contracts for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 were down 2.4% ahead of the open following disappointing earnings reports from the likes of Amazon.com Inc and Intel Corp.

Bitcoin had hovered around US$80,000 for much of the week. However, a Friday expiry of US$11 billion worth of options on the platform Deribit loomed over the market, adding to the broader risk-off mood. About US$1.3 billion worth of bullish positions on cryptocurrencies were wiped out in a 24-hour period, according to Coinglass data.

“The downside is the series of body blows to crypto infrastructure over recent months could dissuade market entrants,” said Noelle Acheson, who writes the Crypto is Macro Now newsletter. “We have seen that self-custody isn’t safe, exchange custody isn’t safe, and the swarm of AI bot attacks on security in all online applications is going to make everyone even more nervous.”

See also: Binance says US$6.3 bil impacted as crypto reels from hack

The upside, however, is that “every new security breach does make security stronger”, she added.

title: China’s mega banks report profit jumps as margins recover
article:
(Oct 30): China’s mega banks reported their biggest quarterly profit increases in recent years as they reined in bad loans and interest margins recovered from record lows.

At Industrial & Commercial Bank of China Ltd, the nation’s largest lender, profit in the third quarter rose 10% to 111.96 billion yuan. That was the biggest gain in five years.

Net income at Agricultural Bank of China Ltd rose 11% and Bank of Communications Co saw a rise of 10.1%. China Construction Bank Corp posted an 9.8% increase and Bank of China Ltd reported a 6.4% gain.

The performance suggests the worst of the profitability crunch may be behind the state commercial banking sector, which has spent years absorbing the financial costs of supporting a slowing economy and an ongoing real estate downturn.

State banks have played a central role as economic shock absorbers, trimming mortgage rates, extending credit to troubled property developers, and pumping loans into government-backed manufacturing and green energy sectors.

That mandate triggered sharp declines in net interest margins, driving industry-wide margins well below the 1.8% threshold historically viewed by regulators as necessary to sustain healthy capitalisation.

See also: PBOC reveals overnight rate at 1.25% before policy anchor shift

ICBC’s net interest margin (NIM), a key gauge of profitability, improved one basis point to 1.29%, after posting steep drops earlier.

Asset quality held largely steady across the major lenders, with bad-loan ratios remaining contained.

See also: BYD earnings dampen hopes Chinese car stocks will reverse rout

Beijing is providing another round of capital support for its state-backed financial giants, with the Ministry of Finance selling 300 billion yuan in special bonds to replenish core Tier 1 capital at eight institutions, including ICBC and Agricultural Bank. The two lenders plan to raise as much as 260 billion yuan combined, with the bulk provided by the ministry.

The move follows a 520 billion yuan recapitalisation in 2025, meaning all six of China’s biggest state lenders have now received support.

For China’s banking sector, the core challenge is pivoting from capital adequacy to capital productivity. Following years of rapid balance-sheet expansion and fresh rounds of state-backed recapitalisation, lenders must now prove they can convert thicker buffers into sustainable returns on equity without taking on outsized credit or market risk.

title: PBOC reveals overnight rate at 1.25% before policy anchor shift
article:
(Oct 30): China’s central bank announced the rate on its overnight reverse repurchase agreements is lower than its current seven-day benchmark, after unveiling plans to adopt it as the main policy lever.

The rate is currently 1.25%, compared with 1.4% on the current seven-day benchmark, according to a statement from the People’s Bank of China (PBOC) on Friday. While the PBOC hasn’t previously made public the rate at which overnight reverse repurchase agreements were conducted, it was set at 1.25% during the first such operation in June, Bloomberg News reported at the time.

The central bank will start to conduct overnight reverse repo operations every day starting from Nov 2, and reduce the frequency of its seven-day reverse repo transactions, it said. The latter will only be used during stretches such as tax payment times and end of month periods.

Earlier in October, the PBOC gave the clearest signal yet of plans to revamp its toolkit by shifting from the seven-day reverse repo rate to the overnight one. The move would be part of a decades-long effort to reform China’s interest-rate system from a centrally planned framework, and better align the PBOC with other major central banks.

Some analysts expected the switch in the main policy lever to take months, since the PBOC will likely need to gradually increase the frequency of the overnight liquidity operation.

title: AI darling Taiwan extends economic growth run unseen since 1987
article:
(Oct 30): Taiwan reported its fourth straight quarter of double-digit economic growth, the longest such stretch in nearly 39 years, as the artificial intelligence (AI) boom increasingly spills over into stronger domestic demand.

Gross domestic product (GDP) expanded 14.36% in the third quarter from a year earlier, according to a statement from the statistics bureau in Taipei on Friday. That exceeded all but one forecast in a Bloomberg survey of economists, whose median estimate was 12%.

Gross capital formation, a measure of investment used to calculate GDP, surged over 26% — the most in five years — with growth in private consumption holding above 5%. Domestic demand contributed more than nine percentage points to last quarter’s growth, with net exports accounting for slightly less than five percentage points.

“Taiwan’s economy remained exceptionally strong,” said Michelle Lam, Greater China economist at Societe Generale. “AI remained the central growth engine, but the impulse is increasingly broad-based. Strong AI demand continued to support exports while driving a surge in domestic capex.”

Home to key suppliers of tech giants like Nvidia Corp and Apple Inc, Taiwan has been one of the biggest beneficiaries of the spread of artificial intelligence. The island’s exports surged almost 61% to a record of over US$87 billion ($111 billion) in September, beating the forecasts of all economists surveyed by Bloomberg.

See also: Lagarde downplays inflation risk as ECB holds, announces her early exit

“Inventories made a positive contribution, but the bigger driver came from private investment,” said Chiang Hsin-yi, an official from the statistics bureau. Private investment has been fuelled by robust exports, she said, adding that the economy is now seeing strength on both the domestic and external fronts.

Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, the world’s largest contract maker of advanced chips, also delivered a better-than-expected revenue outlook for the fourth quarter after reporting a 69% jump in profit for July to September, even as concerns persist over whether the AI investment boom can be sustained.

The rapid expansion has also bolstered Taiwan’s public finances. The cabinet proposed a record NT$3.93 trillion (US$120 billion or $150 billion) spending plan for 2027, giving the government more room to fund priorities including defence. Under the proposal, overall military spending would exceed 3% of GDP.

See also: Race to replace Lagarde begins after she announces leaving ECB in early 2027

The strength of the economy could add to the debate over whether Taiwan’s central bank should resume raising interest rates in December, after keeping its benchmark unchanged for 10 consecutive quarters.

Economists at Goldman Sachs Group Inc recently revised their monetary policy call from “an extended hold” and now see a rate hike cycle starting in December 2026.

“Robust growth gives the central bank room to focus on inflation,” said Raymond Yeung, chief economist for Greater China at Australia & New Zealand Banking Group Ltd. “A potential reversal in the AI investment boom poses a key downside risk, although this is not our base case and the timing of any downturn remains highly uncertain.”

title: Britain’s plan to tax its way out of debt tests the limits
article:
(Oct 30): Britain was singled out for praise by the International Monetary Fund (IMF) this month for the boldest deficit-reduction plan of any Group of Seven nation. Bolder still is its decision to deliver the whole squeeze with higher taxes, as economists warn that Chancellor of the Exchequer John Healey is pushing the boundaries of what’s possible.

Over the five years of the current parliamentary term, the government plans to reduce borrowing by £76 billion (US$102 billion or $130 billion). All of that and more, £107 billion in total, will be done through tax hikes, the Resolution Foundation said in its analysis of Wednesday’s budget.

In 2010, the then-Conservative chancellor, George Osborne, split his austerity programme 80:20 between spending and tax as he sought to repair the public finances in the wake of the financial crisis. His Labour predecessor, Alistair Darling, had planned for a 66:34 division.

Healey is pushing the other way at a time when the tax burden is at its highest since the Second World War and living standards are under renewed assault, this time from the energy shock caused by the US-Iran conflict.

Analysis this month by Adam Slater, the lead economist at Oxford Economics, found that while all consolidation programmes have a high failure rate, “the evidence suggests that fiscal adjustments are more likely to succeed if they rely mainly on spending cuts rather than tax rises”.

See also: PM Burnham says he wants UK to rejoin EU in his lifetime

The budget raised taxes by roughly £6 billion a year from 2028 and topped up departmental day-to-day budgets by an average of £3 billion a year. On Thursday, Healey said there are no plans to bring down the hundreds of billions that Britain spends on welfare each year before the next general election, due in 2029.

The approach has opened up Labour to attacks from the opposition Conservative Party. “On the big challenges, what has this budget actually done? It does not reduce borrowing. Total debt has gone up. It does not properly fund defence,” said shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith. “It does not cut taxes to get the economy growing. Instead, they are putting up taxes again.”

His choice of tax levers suggested he is running out options. With his hands tied by Labour’s manifesto pledge not to raise any of the four main tax rates, much of the work was done through administrative tweaks, including powers to deduct funds directly from debtors’ bank accounts.

See also: Axel Springer to cut Telegraph jobs after buying UK newspaper

Additional taxes on savers, landlords and banks raised only £2 billion, and the increased bank surcharge is withdrawn after 15 months. Five of Healey’s measures have a “high degree of uncertainty”, the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) judged.

Rodrigo Valdes, the director of the IMF’s fiscal affairs department, said earlier this month that the UK has raised taxes so much there is little left that does not have side effects. “More revenues is not easy,” he said. “It distorts at the end of the day.”

“There is a limit to how much you can squeeze out of households and businesses before crimping economic growth,” said Paul Dales, the chief UK economist of Capital Economics. “We may have reached that limit.”

Tax receipts climbed to 36% of gross domestic product (GDP) last year and are on course for 38.6% of GDP in 2031-2032, the OBR predicts. Between 1997 when Labour last took power and the eve of the pandemic in 2020, the burden averaged 32.7%. The bulk of the increase is coming through frozen tax thresholds, which have dragged millions of people into paying more tax as their pay rises. A full-time worker on the national minimum wage earning £25,275 is now halfway to paying higher 40% rate of tax.

Tax hikes since 2020 by both the former Conservative government and the current Labour one partly explain the collapse in living standards this decade, Resolution chief executive Ruth Curtice said. Real household disposable incomes are forecast to rise just 1.4% this decade, just a tenth of the growth in the 2010s which itself was the worst decade since at least the 1960s.
